parameters.query:
WITH handover AS (
  SELECT nullif($1::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS item
),
claim AS (
  SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN h.item ->> 'domain_id' ~ '^[0-9]{1,18}$'
      THEN (h.item ->> 'domain_id')::bigint
    END AS domain_id
  FROM handover h
)
-- The first node after the trigger, and the shape the parent design fixes for every
-- workflow in this set (.specs/2026-08-19-research-pipeline-port.md, section 4): the
-- domain's personas and taxonomy, read as ONE query answering exactly one row. Both
-- halves are argued in full on ar-ingest's Load Domain Context, which asks the same
-- question of the same tables and is not repeated here. What is written out below is
-- the half that differs, which is how this canvas gets a domain at all.

-- It is handed one. ar-ingest reads its domain back off the runs row a dispatcher
-- wrote, and ar-capture resolves one through the source a posted envelope claims.
-- This workflow is invoked by both of those, and each of them puts the domain it had
-- already resolved onto the item it hands over. So the resolution happened in the
-- caller, and what is left here is to read the claim and fetch against it.

-- The whole hand-over item binds as ONE jsonb parameter rather than one parameter per
-- member. An item reaching this trigger by hand may be anything at all,
-- JSON.stringify makes every one of those a valid jsonb literal, and the members are
-- then read where a comment can say what each one is instead of inside an expression
-- no gate reads. The nullif is the other half of that: JSON.stringify(null) binds the
-- JSON null literal rather than SQL NULL, so an invocation carrying no item at all
-- would otherwise arrive here as a value.

-- ->> answers NULL for every jsonb that is not an object, so an item that is not one
-- needs no guard in front of the read: the pattern test is handed NULL, the CASE
-- answers NULL, and nothing raises over a shape somebody else chose. It renders a
-- number as text as readily as a string, which is what lets one read cover both
-- spellings an id can arrive in. A bigint projected as a top-level column comes back
-- as a JSON string and one taken out of a jsonb_agg array comes back as a number, and
-- a caller is free to hand over either.

-- The digit bound is {1,18} rather than +, and the difference between them is a
-- raise. A longer run of digits matches + and then overflows the bigint cast, which
-- is an error this node could not survive: eighteen digits sits inside bigint's
-- nineteen, and no domains id is going to reach it.

-- Three readings come out of this row and they are not two. A null domain_id means
-- the item named no domain this statement could read. A domain_id with a null domain
-- means it named one that matches no domains row. A domain row means the pass
-- resolved, and an empty list beside it is a domain that states no personas, no
-- categories, no terms or no criteria. Read them in that order: a length says nothing
-- until both have been read.

-- Nothing here refuses, which is the shape both callers already have. Every finding
-- this pass is asked about is a row somebody else already wrote, so a refusal at the
-- top of this workflow leaves those rows unscored with nothing recording why. What
-- this answers instead is a row saying what it could and could not resolve, and what
-- a pass that resolved nothing records is the closing group's to decide.

-- The hand-over item is not echoed forward whole. This node's answer REPLACES the
-- item the trigger was handed, and what a caller puts on it besides the domain is the
-- subject list and one provenance member: finding_ids says exactly which rows this
-- pass is to score, and ingest_run_id or capture_document_id says which pass wrote
-- them. Whatever node below needs them reaches all of it at
-- $('Execute Workflow Trigger').first().json, which is the handle every node here has
-- on the invocation, and reading that list is the selection group's rather than this
-- node's. domain_id travels because it is the parameter rather than a column read
-- back, so it survives an item that resolved to nothing.

-- Every list is ordered, which nothing downstream requires and every reader benefits
-- from: two passes over one unchanged domain hand the nodes below the same lists in
-- the same order, so a diff between two runs is about the findings rather than about
-- the order a planner happened to return rows in.
SELECT
  (SELECT domain_id FROM claim) AS domain_id,

  -- The domain row, cut to the members the nodes below read. feature_version is the
  -- one that has to travel: Compute Feature Vectors holds the version it composes
  -- from this domain's terms against domains.feature_version and carries the answer
  -- forward, so fetching that one integer separately would be the lookup node this
  -- shape exists to avoid. It travels as a report rather than as the key. What that
  -- node skips a recomputation on is the document's own stored version held against
  -- the composed one, and its body says why the domain's pin cannot be what a skip is
  -- decided on. NULL rather than an empty object when the item named no domain this
  -- statement could resolve, which is the second of the three readings above.
  (SELECT jsonb_build_object(
     'id', d.id,
     'slug', d.slug,
     'name', d.name,
     'settings', d.settings,
     'feature_version', d.feature_version,
     'embedding_model', d.embedding_model)
     FROM domains d
    WHERE d.id = (SELECT domain_id FROM claim)) AS domain,

  -- The personas. system_text is operator-owned prose and is the trusted half of what
  -- prompt-frame.ts composes around an untrusted chunk. No node on this canvas makes
  -- a model call and none is planned to: what scores a finding here is criteria rows,
  -- terms and deterministic libraries, which is what lets a score be reproduced from
  -- the rows it was read against. They are selected because the design fixes personas
  -- and taxonomy as what this node fetches, and because a canvas that grows a judging
  -- step should not grow a second lookup with it.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', p.id,
       'role', p.role,
       'system_text', p.system_text)
       ORDER BY p.role, p.id)
       FROM personas p
      WHERE p.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM claim)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS personas,

  -- The categories, which are the buckets the terms below are filed under. key rather
  -- than id is what a reader downstream matches on: features.ts builds a column name
  -- out of it and static-gate.ts groups hits by it, so the surrogate id travels for
  -- an operator's benefit and the key is what the libraries read.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', c.id,
       'key', c.key,
       'name', c.name,
       'parent_id', c.parent_id)
       ORDER BY c.key, c.id)
       FROM categories c
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM claim)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS categories,

  -- The terms, joined to their category's key rather than carrying category_id. Four
  -- members and this exact spelling, because the libraries reading this one list each
  -- read a different subset of it: features.ts takes pattern and category,
  -- feature-version.ts takes all four, and static-gate.ts takes pattern, weight and
  -- polarity. A term list selected without the join satisfies one reader and starves
  -- the others, with nothing failing.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'category', c.key,
       'pattern', t.pattern,
       'weight', t.weight,
       'polarity', t.polarity)
       ORDER BY c.key, t.pattern, t.id)
       FROM terms t
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = t.category_id
      WHERE c.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM claim)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS terms,

  -- The criteria, joined to their category the same way. This is the workflow they
  -- were being fetched for: ar-ingest and ar-capture both select them, and both say
  -- the same thing about them, that they are ar-score's subject and that nothing on
  -- those canvases reads them. Here they are what the pass is about. value is what
  -- the domain stated and kind is which way the statement points, and what a kind
  -- means for a score is the scoring group's to state rather than this node's.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', k.id,
       'category', c.key,
       'value', k.value,
       'kind', k.kind)
       ORDER BY c.key, k.kind, k.id)
       FROM criteria k
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = k.category_id
      WHERE k.domain_id = (SELECT domain_id FROM claim)),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS criteria

WITH
-- The subjects, and what they are scored against. One item per finding the caller
-- named, with the document behind it and the domain's stated criteria beside it,
-- which between them are the whole of what the groups below read. The node above
-- answered the domain; this one answers what the pass is about.

-- ONE ITEM PER FINDING, and every group below this one is built on that. A Postgres
-- node maps its statement over the items it was handed and passes on what the
-- statement returned, so this node takes the one context item above it and answers as
-- many items as the hand over named findings. The feature group computes a vector per
-- document and the scoring group writes a score per finding, so each of them is one
-- item's work and neither has to loop.

-- Which also means this node's answer REPLACES the context item, the way that item
-- replaced the one the trigger was handed. The personas, the categories and the terms
-- are not gone: a node below reaches them as $('Load Domain Context').first().json,
-- which is the handle ar-ingest's own source selection leaves its canvas. The
-- criteria are the exception and travel on every item, for the reason the projection
-- below gives.

-- THE CRITERIA ARE READ TWICE ON THIS CANVAS AND THE TWO READS ARE NOT ONE LIST. Load
-- Domain Context answers the domain's taxonomy whole, which is what the design fixes
-- for the first node after every trigger, and a criterion nobody has filled in
-- belongs in that answer: the row says the domain has raised the question. This read
-- is the scoring one and it drops exactly those rows. criteria.value in
-- src/db/schema/taxonomy.ts states the rule and the reason: an empty value is an
-- unfilled criterion rather than a stated blank, and read as a value under a bucket
-- that excludes things it says exclude everything, which is the opposite of what
-- leaving it blank meant. So the shorter list is what a score may be taken against
-- and the longer one is the domain's whole statement. Nothing here reconciles them,
-- because they answer different questions.

-- EVERY CRITERION CARRIES ITS CATEGORY KEY, and that join is what the port bought.
-- The design this one is ported from filed a criterion under a text column
-- constrained to a fixed vocabulary, which put the list of buckets in DDL: adding one
-- meant dropping the constraint and re-adding it widened. Here a category is a row in
-- a table the domain already owns and criteria.category_id points at it, so this
-- statement is what reads that migration's result. c.key is what a bucket is known by
-- from outside the table, it is what features.ts builds a column name out of, and it
-- is therefore what lets a reading taken over a document be matched to what the
-- domain stated about the bucket that reading falls in. The surrogate id travels
-- beside it for an operator's benefit and nothing below matches on it.

-- NO LIMIT, and its absence is a decision rather than an omission. The design this
-- one is ported from capped this selection at a fixed number of rows because every
-- row it returned became a model call, so the cap was a cost ceiling and not paging.
-- Nothing on this canvas calls a model: what scores a finding here is criteria rows,
-- terms and deterministic libraries, so a row costs arithmetic and a row left out
-- costs a finding its score. What bounds the pass is the caller, which hands over
-- exactly the findings it wrote.

-- TWO PARAMETERS, in declaration order: the hand over item and the domain. The hand
-- over binds whole as ONE jsonb value rather than one parameter per member, for the
-- reason Load Domain Context gives: an item reaching this trigger by hand may be
-- anything at all, JSON.stringify makes every one of those a valid jsonb literal, and
-- the nullif is what keeps JSON.stringify(null) from arriving as the JSON null
-- literal rather than as SQL NULL. The domain is read off the context item rather
-- than out of the hand over a second time. That node has already resolved it, and
-- deriving it a second way here is how the two start being able to disagree.

-- AN ID IS READ AS TEXT AND NEVER BY TYPE, which is the reading this statement cannot
-- take on trust. finding_ids arrives from two callers that build it two ways:
-- ar-ingest aggregates ids it read back off its own insert and ar-capture builds a
-- one element array out of a column, so an element can be a JSON number or a JSON
-- string and a jsonb_typeof test matches one spelling while dropping the other. #>>
-- renders both as text and answers NULL for a JSON null, so one predicate covers a
-- number, a string, an absent element and something that is not an id at all. The
-- digit bound is {1,18} rather than +: a longer run matches + and then overflows the
-- bigint cast, which is a raise over a list somebody else built.

-- THREE THINGS REACH ZERO ROWS HERE and this statement parts none of them: a hand
-- over naming no finding, a domain that resolved to nothing, and findings filed under
-- some other domain than the one the pass claims. A node handed no item does not run,
-- so all three end the pass above the group that would account for it, which is the
-- canvas topology's to answer rather than this statement's. What keeps it readable
-- from outside is that the hand over stays where it arrived: the length of
-- finding_ids held against the number of items this node answered says how many named
-- findings were scored, and the closing group is where that comparison belongs.
handover AS (
  SELECT nullif($1::jsonb, 'null'::jsonb) AS item
),

-- The findings the caller named, read off the hand over rather than out of a
-- predicate. Nothing here decides which findings are worth scoring: ar-ingest hands
-- over the findings its pass wrote and ar-capture the one its capture produced, and a
-- workflow that went looking for unscored rows of its own would be scoring a corpus
-- nobody asked it about.

-- DISTINCT because a repeated id would score one finding twice and write its row
-- twice, and a caller building the list out of a stream is the shape that produces
-- one. The pattern test and the cast sit in one CTE, so what the outer query joins on
-- is a list of ids rather than whatever the hand over held: an element the test
-- refused never reaches the cast, and one that reaches it is inside the bound the
-- header above gives.
subject AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT (e.value #>> '{}')::bigint AS finding_id
  FROM handover h,
       jsonb_array_elements(
         CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(h.item -> 'finding_ids') = 'array'
              THEN h.item -> 'finding_ids'
              ELSE '[]'::jsonb
         END) AS e(value)
  WHERE (e.value #>> '{}') ~ '^[0-9]{1,18}$'
)

SELECT
  -- The finding, cut to the members the groups below read. score and score_version
  -- travel as a pair because they are written as one: a stored score is stale exactly
  -- when its version is behind the scorer's, and a score carrying no version reads as
  -- scored to everything looking for a number with no version for a re-score to find
  -- it stale by. Both are null for a finding nothing has scored, which is the
  -- ordinary state of every finding a caller has just written, and findings.score is
  -- where the null-vs-zero rule is stated: a number computed from data is absent
  -- rather than zero when nothing measured it.

  -- fields is the domain's own half of the finding, validated on the way in against
  -- DomainSettings.fieldContract and holding exactly the members that contract names.
  -- It travels because a reading about the finding rather than about its document
  -- would be taken over it, and because fetching it again from a node that already
  -- holds the finding id would be the second lookup this projection exists to avoid.

  -- entity_id is the subject this finding was attributed to, or null for one nothing
  -- attributed, which findings.entity_id calls an ordinary state rather than an edge
  -- case. It travels for the closing group, which raises research intentions over the
  -- subjects this pass found worth researching and files a row under the entity where
  -- there is one.
  f.id AS finding_id,
  f.domain_id,
  f.document_id,
  f.entity_id,
  f.fields,
  f.score,
  f.score_version,

  -- The document behind it, and this join can drop nothing. findings.document_id is
  -- NOT NULL with a foreign key onto documents, so every finding has exactly one and
  -- an inner join is the shape that says so. A LEFT JOIN here would suggest a finding
  -- can stand without the material it was read out of, which this schema does not
  -- admit.

  -- body is what a vector is computed over and what a term is matched against.
  -- parse_status travels beside it because a document whose parse failed still has a
  -- row and may still have an empty body, and a vector of zeros taken over one is a
  -- reading nobody took: the group that computes it has to be able to say which of
  -- the two it is looking at.

  -- features and feature_version are the stored vector and the version it was read
  -- against, and the pair is what the feature group skips on. A document whose stored
  -- version already equals the version composed for this domain is left alone, so
  -- both have to be here for that comparison to be made without a second SELECT. Null
  -- for a document nothing has featurized, which is the absence that column reserves
  -- rather than a zero.
  d.body AS document_body,
  d.parse_status AS document_parse_status,
  d.features AS document_features,
  d.feature_version AS document_feature_version,

  -- The criteria, joined to the category key each one hangs off and cut to the rows
  -- that state something. The header above says how this read differs from the
  -- taxonomy read one node up and why both are correct. The subquery is uncorrelated
  -- with the finding, so the planner reads the table once however many findings the
  -- pass names, and the list travels on every item because a Code node below scores
  -- one finding against the whole stated position and a score has to be a function of
  -- the item it is written for.

  -- kind is which way the statement points and value is what the domain stated. Both
  -- travel and neither filters: a refusal dropped from the read, or presented as
  -- background, is the domain's clearest signal arriving as its vaguest, which is
  -- what criteria.kind says about itself. What a kind means for a score is the
  -- scoring group's to state rather than this node's.

  -- Ordered the way the node above orders its own criteria, so the two lists can be
  -- read beside each other. An empty list is a domain that has stated nothing, and it
  -- is what a scoring pass over a domain nobody has configured is scoring against.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(jsonb_build_object(
       'id', k.id,
       'category', c.key,
       'value', k.value,
       'kind', k.kind)
       ORDER BY c.key, k.kind, k.id)
       FROM criteria k
       JOIN categories c ON c.id = k.category_id
      WHERE k.domain_id = $2::bigint
        AND btrim(k.value) <> ''),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS criteria
FROM findings f
JOIN subject s ON s.finding_id = f.id
JOIN documents d ON d.id = f.document_id
-- The domain the context node resolved, and the predicate is what keeps a pass inside
-- one domain's taxonomy. A finding names its own domain, and scoring one against
-- another domain's criteria would be a number computed from a position nobody holds,
-- so a named finding filed elsewhere is not scored here. A NULL domain selects
-- nothing, which is where a pass started by hand ends.

-- Ordered by id, which nothing below requires and every reader benefits from, for the
-- reason the lists in the node above are ordered: two passes over one unchanged
-- domain hand the groups below the same findings in the same order, so a diff between
-- two runs is about the scores rather than about the order a planner happened to
-- return rows in.
WHERE f.domain_id = $2::bigint
ORDER BY f.id

WITH
-- Where a score and the version that dates it become one row, together or not at all.
-- findings.score and findings.score_version are written by a single statement because
-- the schema asks for exactly that: a score stored with a null version reads as
-- scored to everything looking for a number, and there is no version for a re-score
-- to find it stale by, so it survives every pass the pin exists to trigger.

-- ONE PARAMETER, the item itself, which is the shape every write in this set uses.
-- Fewer values for the comma splitter to get wrong than a member per column, and the
-- members are read out below where a comment can say what each one is instead of
-- inside an expression no gate reads.

-- ONE ROW OUT PER ITEM. The update sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT reads the row
-- the parameter made, so this node answers exactly one item for every item it was
-- handed whether or not the update matched anything. An UPDATE ... RETURNING on its
-- own would emit nothing where it matched nothing, and the item would leave the
-- stream at exactly the point where the write not landing is the thing worth
-- reporting: a finding nothing could measure is an ordinary outcome of this group
-- rather than a fault in it.
item AS (
  SELECT $1::jsonb AS payload
),

-- The members, cast once. The ids arrive as the node above carried them and are not
-- re-derived here, which is the rule every node on this canvas follows. They take a
-- bare cast rather than a digit pattern because none of them came off the hand-over:
-- every one was projected by Select Scoring Subjects out of a column, and the pattern
-- tests on this canvas guard the members a caller wrote.

-- score and score_version are read through a pattern because they were computed
-- rather than read back, and the pattern is what makes the cast safe on a value that
-- is not a number. A total that overflowed to an infinity is stringified as the JSON
-- null literal and answers NULL here, and so does anything else that is not a bounded
-- run of digits. The sign is admitted because a scheme carrying a penalty can put a
-- total below zero, which aggregate-score.ts states rather than bounds.
reading AS (
  SELECT
    (i.payload ->> 'finding_id')::bigint AS finding_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'domain_id')::bigint AS domain_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'document_id')::bigint AS document_id,
    (i.payload ->> 'entity_id')::bigint AS entity_id,
    CASE WHEN (i.payload ->> 'score') ~ '^-?[0-9]{1,15}$'
         THEN (i.payload ->> 'score')::numeric
    END AS score,
    CASE WHEN (i.payload ->> 'score_version') ~ '^[0-9]{1,9}$'
         THEN (i.payload ->> 'score_version')::integer
    END AS score_version,
    (i.payload ->> 'score_signals_stated')::integer AS score_signals_stated,
    (i.payload ->> 'score_signals_measured')::integer AS score_signals_measured,
    (i.payload ->> 'feature_version')::integer AS feature_version,
    (i.payload ->> 'feature_version_matches_domain')::boolean
      AS feature_version_matches_domain
  FROM item i
),

-- The write, and the pair is the whole of it. Both columns are set or neither is,
-- which is what the WHERE enforces: an item carrying no score, or no version to date
-- one with, updates nothing and comes back saying so. That is the null-vs-zero rule
-- reaching the row, and findings.score is the column that states it.

-- Nothing else on the row is touched. The domain, the document, the entity and the
-- fields payload were settled by whichever workflow wrote the finding, and a scorer
-- rewriting any of them would be answering a question nobody asked it.

-- A RE-SCORE THAT MEASURES NOTHING LEAVES THE PREVIOUS NUMBER STANDING. The guard
-- reads this pass's answer rather than the row, so a finding scored under an earlier
-- scheme keeps that score and that version when a later pass finds nothing to
-- measure. Blanking it would discard a reading somebody took in favour of one nobody
-- did, and the version beside it still names the scheme that produced it.

-- No ON CONFLICT and no guard against running twice over one finding, the id being
-- the key and an UPDATE being idempotent: the same item written a second time stores
-- the same score under the same version.
written AS (
  UPDATE findings f
     SET score = r.score,
         score_version = r.score_version
    FROM reading r
   WHERE f.id = r.finding_id
     AND r.score IS NOT NULL
     AND r.score_version IS NOT NULL
  RETURNING f.id
)

SELECT
  -- The item this node answers, which is about the finding rather than about the
  -- write. The ids travel because the group that closes this pass reads its counts
  -- off what came through here, and entity_id travels because that group files a
  -- research intention under the subject a finding was attributed to.
  r.finding_id,
  r.domain_id,
  r.document_id,
  r.entity_id,
  r.score,
  r.score_version,

  -- score_signals_stated and score_signals_measured are the account of a score that
  -- no column holds, and they ride rather than land. The first is how many buckets
  -- the domain stated a position under and the second how many of those the vector
  -- held a cell for, so the pair is what tells a domain that has configured nothing
  -- apart from a corpus that matched nothing.
  r.score_signals_stated,
  r.score_signals_measured,

  -- feature_version and feature_version_matches_domain are carried through unchanged
  -- from the node above, which composed the first and held it against
  -- domains.feature_version to get the second. Nothing here acts on either and no
  -- column stores them: they reach the closing group so an execution can say what
  -- generation of vectors this pass scored against.
  r.feature_version,
  r.feature_version_matches_domain,

  -- finding_scored is whether the update matched a row. False for an item that
  -- carried no score to write, and false is the whole of what this column says: why a
  -- score is absent sits on the two counts above and on the item the node above
  -- built, findings having nowhere to put an account of a score that was not taken.
  (SELECT w.id FROM written w) IS NOT NULL AS finding_scored
FROM reading r

WITH
-- Where a finding becomes an intention to research its subject, and the only row this
-- pass writes that a person has to rule on before anything acts on it. research_pool
-- in src/db/schema/entities.ts is that gate, and its whole argument is that noticing
-- a subject is worth looking into and actually looking are separate events, written
-- by different things at different times. This node is the noticing half. Nothing
-- here searches anything, and nothing here approves anything.

-- IT IS THE ONLY RAISE ON THE PUSH PATH AND A SECOND ONE ON THE PULL PATH, which is
-- why it sits here rather than on either caller. ar-ingest raises its own intentions
-- before it invokes this workflow and ar-capture raises none at all, so the two paths
-- converge on this canvas and one node covers both. On the pull path this pass
-- usually raises nothing: every finding ar-ingest already covered is turned away by
-- the NOT EXISTS below, which is the guard that node was written for and says so in
-- as many words. On the push path this is where a captured finding becomes an
-- intention or never becomes one.

-- THE SCORE DOES NOT GATE IT, and that is a decision rather than an omission. A
-- cutoff needs a threshold and there is nowhere to declare one: DomainSettings in
-- src/db/schema/domains.ts declares four members and no threshold of any kind, and
-- the scale a domain writes its weights on is open, which aggregate-score.ts records
-- as the port's open scale question. A number written here would be one nobody
-- stated. The stronger half is what the nodes above already say about a null score:
-- three of the ways a finding goes unscored are facts about the domain's
-- configuration rather than about the finding, so a raise gated on the score would
-- stop raising intentions for a domain that had misconfigured itself, and would do it
-- silently. The score is reported by the group that closes this pass and filters
-- nothing here.

-- WHAT IT DOES GATE ON is the rule ar-ingest applies, spelled the same way on
-- purpose: a finding carrying a string somebody could search for, and no intention
-- already citing it. research_pool.search_terms records why the first matters, an
-- empty list being storable and the drain meeting one closing the row rather than
-- searching for nothing, which is a row an operator ruled on for no reason.

-- THE TERMS ARE THE FINDING'S OWN STRINGS, read back off the payload rather than
-- composed here. findings.fields holds exactly the members
-- DomainSettings.fieldContract declares and exactly the types it declared them at,
-- whichever caller wrote the row having refused any answer whose member was the wrong
-- shape and dropped any member the contract does not name. So jsonb_typeof over the
-- stored payload IS that contract as it was applied, and reading it that way rather
-- than fetching settings.fieldContract again is what keeps this statement from
-- carrying a second copy of a rule able to stop agreeing with the first.

-- EACH TERM IS TRIMMED, DEDUPLICATED, ORDERED, AND DROPPED IF IT IS LONG. Trimming is
-- what makes the deduplication do real work: two spellings of one word differing only
-- in whitespace are one thing to search for and two lines in a listing an operator
-- reads. The bound is 80 characters, which is MAX_ENTITY_NAME_LENGTH in
-- src/lib/validate-entity-name.ts. A value past it is an extraction that has turned
-- into a payload rather than a name, which is that module's own reading of the same
-- number, and that module is the capability gate these strings meet again in
-- ar-research's Gate Candidate Names, landed in phase 6, before any of them reaches a
-- request. The number is written out here because a statement can splice nothing; the
-- module is where it is declared and where the argument for it lives.

-- entity_id IS CARRIED RATHER THAN READ BACK, and that is what Select Scoring
-- Subjects says it travels for. The join below reaches the same column and could
-- answer it, and reading it there would be a second derivation able to disagree with
-- the one the pass reported: the window is one pass wide and what an intention names
-- should be the subject the pass was scoring. NULL is an ordinary answer rather than
-- a gap. research_pool.entity_id records that an intention raised from a finding
-- whose subject nothing has attributed is a row like any other, and that the terms
-- are what makes it researchable anyway; what it refuses is the alternative, one
-- placeholder entity standing for every unnamed subject there is.

-- status takes its pending default, the only state a row nobody has looked at can
-- honestly hold, and approved_at and researched_at are left null, which is where the
-- gate wants them and where research_pool_approval_check holds them.

-- ONE INTENTION PER FINDING, and the NOT EXISTS below is the whole of the
-- deduplication. research_pool carries no unique key and could not be given one over
-- two nullable columns, so deduplicating is the writer's, which that table says in as
-- many words. The predicate is spelled exactly as ar-ingest spells its own, so the
-- two writers cannot come to disagree about what a duplicate is. It is a read of the
-- snapshot this statement began under, so two passes raising for one finding at the
-- same instant is a race nothing here closes; the cost of losing it is a duplicate in
-- a queue rather than a duplicate search.

-- ONE ROW OUT, whatever was raised. The insert sits in a CTE and the outer SELECT
-- names no FROM, so this node answers exactly one item however many rows it wrote,
-- including none. Close Score Run below is built on that, and reads both lists this
-- node answers by name.

-- RUNS ONCE FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, so it runs against the
-- first item it was handed and reads the findings off Write Finding Scores by name.
-- The stream arriving here is one item per finding scored, and a statement mapped
-- over it would raise this pass's intentions once for every finding in it. No gate in
-- this repository reads a node-level property, so nothing reports that setting going
-- missing except the duplicates this statement's own NOT EXISTS then turns away.

-- AN ID IS TESTED AS TEXT AND NEVER BY TYPE. A bigint read as a top-level column
-- comes back off the driver as a STRING, so Write Finding Scores answers a finding_id
-- spelled "41" while an id taken out of a jsonb_agg array elsewhere on this canvas
-- arrives as the number 41. A predicate written on jsonb_typeof would match one
-- spelling and silently drop the other. The regex below reads the TEXT of the member,
-- which is the same for both spellings and is NULL for an absent member and for a
-- JSON null, so one predicate covers a projection that stopped carrying the member
-- and anything that is not an id at all.

-- ONE PARAMETER, the findings this pass scored as Write Finding Scores answered them.
-- One value rather than one per member leaves the comma splitter nothing to get
-- wrong, and an array is what a jsonb function reads.

-- The findings, as Write Finding Scores answered them. That node emits one item for
-- every item it was handed whether or not it wrote a score, so this list is the
-- findings the pass reached rather than the findings it measured, which is the
-- distinction the header argues.
item AS (
  SELECT $1::jsonb AS payload
),

-- The ids and the subjects, read as text for the reason the header gives. A member
-- that is absent, a JSON null, or something that is not an id at all fails the same
-- predicate, so one test covers all three. DISTINCT because a repeated finding would
-- be considered twice and, on the first pass over it, raised twice: the NOT EXISTS
-- below reads a snapshot taken before this statement's own insert and cannot see a
-- row this statement is in the middle of writing.
finding AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT
    (w.value ->> 'finding_id')::bigint AS finding_id,
    CASE WHEN (w.value ->> 'entity_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
         THEN (w.value ->> 'entity_id')::bigint
    END AS entity_id
  FROM item i,
       jsonb_array_elements(
         CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(i.payload) = 'array'
              THEN i.payload
              ELSE '[]'::jsonb
         END) AS w(value)
  WHERE (w.value ->> 'finding_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
),

-- The rows themselves, read back rather than carried. The parameter carries ids and
-- nothing else, the expression above cutting each item down to the two members this
-- statement reads, and what the terms are read out of is the payload as it was
-- stored, so this join is what puts the two together. domain_id comes off the finding
-- rather than off the pass: an intention is filed under the domain of the finding
-- that raised it, which is the same domain this pass ran for and is read from the row
-- that is actually being cited.

-- The terms. A member the contract declared as anything other than a string has no
-- spelling a search could be issued with, and a member the answer never stated is not
-- in the payload at all, so one type test covers both. The CASE around the payload is
-- not defensive dressing: jsonb_each raises on a value that is not an object,
-- findings.fields is NOT NULL with a {} default and can hold any JSON a writer put
-- there, and a raise here would leave the pass with no account of itself, the node
-- that writes one sitting below this one.

-- The empty list is what a finding with nothing searchable comes to, and it is the
-- value the insert filters on rather than a row anybody stores.
subject AS (
  SELECT
    f.id,
    f.domain_id,
    n.entity_id,
    COALESCE(
      (SELECT jsonb_agg(DISTINCT t.term ORDER BY t.term)
         FROM (
           SELECT btrim(e.value #>> '{}') AS term
             FROM jsonb_each(
                    CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(f.fields) = 'object'
                         THEN f.fields
                         ELSE '{}'::jsonb
                    END) e
            WHERE jsonb_typeof(e.value) = 'string') t
        WHERE t.term <> ''
          AND length(t.term) <= 80),
      '[]'::jsonb) AS search_terms
  FROM findings f
  JOIN finding n ON n.finding_id = f.id
),

-- The write, and the two predicates are the whole of what it decides. A finding
-- yielding no term raises nothing, and a finding already carrying an intention raises
-- nothing.

-- No ON CONFLICT clause, because there is no key to collide on: research_pool has
-- none and cannot be given one over two nullable columns. The NOT EXISTS above is
-- what stands in its place, and the difference between the two is worth knowing
-- rather than glossing. A unique key refuses at the instant of the write; this reads
-- a snapshot and can be beaten by a concurrent pass.
raised AS (
  INSERT INTO research_pool (domain_id, entity_id, finding_id, search_terms)
  SELECT s.domain_id, s.entity_id, s.id, s.search_terms
  FROM subject s
  WHERE jsonb_array_length(s.search_terms) > 0
    AND NOT EXISTS (
      SELECT 1
      FROM research_pool p
      WHERE p.finding_id = s.id)
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and it is a report rather than a hand-over: nothing
-- below invokes anything, and Close Score Run is the only reader either list has.

-- searchable_finding_ids is every finding this pass could have raised an intention
-- for, which is the shorter list the term rule leaves. intention_ids is what was
-- actually raised, and the difference between the two lengths is the findings an
-- intention already cited: on the pull path that is almost all of them, and saying so
-- is what keeps a run reading zero intentions from looking like a pass that found
-- nothing.

-- Both are lists rather than counts so that Close Score Run tallies them the way it
-- tallies every other node's items, through one reading rather than through a special
-- case. Ordered, so two passes over one unchanged domain report the same lists in the
-- same order.
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(s.id ORDER BY s.id) FROM subject s
      WHERE jsonb_array_length(s.search_terms) > 0),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS searchable_finding_ids,
  COALESCE(
    (SELECT jsonb_agg(r.id ORDER BY r.id) FROM raised r),
    '[]'::jsonb) AS intention_ids

options.queryReplacement: ={{ JSON.stringify($('Write Finding Scores').all().map((item) => ({ finding_id: item.json.finding_id, entity_id: item.json.entity_id }))) }}

parameters.query:
WITH
-- Where the pass says what it did, and the one node on this canvas that writes a runs
-- row at all. runs in src/db/schema/runs.ts keeps that account in three columns
-- because a reader wanting any one of them should not have to parse the other two:
-- status is what the pass came to, counts is what it did, and errors is what it could
-- not do. This statement writes all three and the finish beside them.

-- IT INSERTS WHERE ar-ingest UPDATES, which is ar-capture's shape rather than its own
-- caller's. A dispatched pass arrives with a run id, ar-dispatch having opened the
-- row before it invoked anything. This workflow is invoked by two workflows and
-- neither opens a row for it: ar-ingest's Score Findings says in as many words that
-- the run it hands over is provenance rather than a row this canvas may write to, and
-- that this workflow closes one of its own. So the row is written once, here, already
-- closed. runs.started_at names exactly this convention as the one the design this
-- port draws from uses, and says that nothing stored tells the two apart. What it
-- costs is the duration: started_at defaults to now() in the same transaction that
-- sets finished_at, so a scoring run reads as instantaneous.

-- A PULL PASS THEREFORE WRITES TWO ROWS, and they are not two accounts of one thing.
-- ar-dispatch opens a row, ar-ingest closes it with what the fetch and the extraction
-- did, and this statement writes a second row with what the scoring did. The counts
-- keys are what tells them apart, a fetch pass tallying documents and this one
-- tallying findings, which is the variation runs.counts is annotated for.

-- SCHEDULED_BY IS operator, AND THE CONVENTION IT BELONGED TO HAS STOPPED
-- DISCRIMINATING. RUN_SCHEDULERS in src/db/schema/values.ts answers who set the
-- next_run_at a run fired against, and a scoring pass fired against none: all three
-- members are wrong of it, and operator is the least wrong, this pass having happened
-- because something acted rather than because a clock came due. ar-capture reached
-- the same answer for the same reason and predicted this node facing the same
-- question. The answer is the same and the cost is that a row saying operator is now
-- a capture or a scoring pass rather than a capture. What still tells those two apart
-- is counts, whose keys are the writer's: a capture row carries captures_received and
-- a scoring row carries findings_handed. The column that would answer it properly, a
-- run naming the workflow that wrote it, is a migration this phase does not carry.

-- WHAT A PASS THAT RESOLVED NOTHING RECORDS, which Load Domain Context left to this
-- group to decide: nothing, and that is a refusal rather than an answer. Every node
-- on this canvas is on one main chain and a node handed no item does not run, so a
-- hand over naming no finding, one naming only findings filed under another domain,
-- and a pass that resolved no domain at all each stop above this node and leave no
-- row behind them. The sticky note over the trigger says the same about the same
-- three shapes. It is named here rather than met because this is the node the cost
-- shows at, and the repair is a branch off the context node, which belongs to the
-- canvas topology rather than to any one group.

-- THE TALLIES ARE COUNTED HERE AND GATHERED THERE. The parameter below carries one
-- array per node, each cut to the members a tally reads, and every rule about what
-- those members MEAN is in this statement: what counts as a finding that was dropped,
-- as a vector that was reused, as a subject nothing could be searched for. An
-- expression can import nothing and is read by no gate in this repository, so a rule
-- written there would be a second copy of something with nowhere to be compared.
-- Naming and projection are what the expression does, and the projection is not
-- cosmetic: the items it reads carry whole feature vectors and whole criteria lists,
-- and binding them unprojected would ship the pass's working back to the database to
-- be counted.

-- THE LISTS ARE NORMALISED AND THE PASS WIDE FACTS ARE READ AS MEMBERS, which is both
-- of the shapes the two sibling workflows use and neither one alone. Every node on
-- this canvas answers one item per finding, so the gathered lists are ar-ingest's
-- shape and a tally is a count with a predicate. The domain and the vector generation
-- are one fact for the whole pass rather than one per finding, so they are read as
-- members the way ar-capture reads its own, and a list of one element repeated per
-- finding would be machinery answering a question that has one answer.

-- AN ID IS TESTED AS TEXT AND NEVER BY TYPE. A bigint read as a top-level column
-- comes back off the driver as a STRING, so every id gathered below arrives spelled
-- "41" while an integer column arrives as the number 41. A test written on
-- jsonb_typeof would answer for one spelling and miss the other, which is a count
-- wrong by a plausible amount rather than one that fails. Every id predicate below
-- reads the member's TEXT, which is the same either way and is NULL for an absent
-- member and for a JSON null. A boolean is compared as jsonb, which needs no cast at
-- all, and every one of those comparisons is wrapped in a COALESCE: a member that
-- never arrived compares to UNKNOWN, and UNKNOWN in the status CASE below would fall
-- through to a branch nobody chose.

-- NOTHING HERE CAN RAISE, which matters more at this node than anywhere else on the
-- canvas: this is where the pass records itself, and a statement that threw would
-- leave a scoring pass with no account at all. So the gathered object is guarded
-- before it is read, jsonb_each and jsonb_array_elements are handed a CASE rather
-- than a member somebody else built, and every cast sits behind a pattern test.

-- WHAT MAKES A PASS partial, failed OR ok. RUN_STATUSES in src/db/schema/values.ts
-- argues partial as the member fail-flag-keep needs: a pass that produced real work
-- and a real failure at once, where either neighbour loses half of it. Read onto a
-- scoring pass, it is a pass that scored some of the findings it was handed and not
-- others. failed is the narrower case where there is no half to keep, a pass that
-- reached findings and measured none of them. A domain that has stated no criteria
-- reaches that outcome every pass, and reporting it is the point: the entry beside it
-- carries the two signal counts, which say whether the domain stated nothing or
-- stated buckets its own terms never name.

-- WHAT DOES NOT MAKE IT partial is a finding whose score this pass left standing. The
-- write above is guarded on this pass's answer rather than on the row, so a finding
-- scored under an earlier scheme keeps that score, and a pass that measured nothing
-- new about it has not lost anything. That is counted, under findings_unscored, and
-- counting it is what a tally is for.

-- THE ERRORS ENTRIES ARE ONE PER FAILURE and are ASSIGNED rather than appended.
-- runs.errors defaults to an empty list and this row is new, so there is nobody
-- else's account of the same run to drop: ar-ingest appends because ar-dispatch
-- opened its row and may write to it. Every value that reaches this column is a count
-- or a node name written here, so nothing read out of a document or posted by a
-- stranger can arrive in it.

-- THE VECTOR GENERATION IS ON THE ANSWER AND NOT IN counts. Write Finding Scores
-- carries the composed feature version and whether it matches the domain's pin, and
-- says they travel so an execution can say what generation of vectors this pass
-- scored against. An execution is where they land: runs.counts is annotated as a map
-- of counts and a version is not one, and no column on runs holds it. Nothing here
-- acts on either, and a mismatch is the ordinary state today, nothing in this
-- pipeline setting domains.feature_version at all.

-- RUNS ONCE FOR THE PASS. executeOnce is set on this node, and the node above already
-- answers exactly one item, so this is a backstop rather than the mechanism.
-- ar-capture sets it on its own closing node for the same reason.

-- ONE PARAMETER, the gathered pass. One value rather than one per node leaves the
-- comma splitter nothing to get wrong, and there is no second value to bind: this
-- workflow invokes nothing, so there is no sub-workflow error to carry the way both
-- callers carry this workflow's own.

-- The gathered pass, guarded before anything reads it. An expression that answered
-- something other than an object leaves every tally below at nought rather than
-- raising.
pass AS (
  SELECT
    CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof($1::jsonb) = 'object'
         THEN $1::jsonb
         ELSE '{}'::jsonb
    END AS nodes
),

-- The facts that are one per pass rather than one per finding, read as members. The
-- domain is the one the context node resolved rather than the one the hand over
-- claimed, those two having already been reconciled two nodes up. It is NULL only for
-- a pass that reached this node without one, which the header says cannot happen from
-- this canvas, and on runs a NULL domain means the pass was not scoped to a domain
-- rather than that one is missing.
scope AS (
  SELECT
    p.nodes,
    CASE WHEN (p.nodes #>> '{context,domain_id}') ~ '^[0-9]{1,18}$'
         THEN (p.nodes #>> '{context,domain_id}')::bigint
    END AS domain_id,
    CASE WHEN (p.nodes #>> '{generation,feature_version}') ~ '^[0-9]{1,9}$'
         THEN (p.nodes #>> '{generation,feature_version}')::integer
    END AS feature_version,
    COALESCE(p.nodes #> '{generation,matches_domain}' = 'true'::jsonb, false)
      AS feature_version_matches_domain
  FROM pass p
),

-- The gathered lists, one row per item with the node it came from beside it.
-- jsonb_each raises on a value that is not an object and jsonb_array_elements on one
-- that is not an array, so both are guarded rather than trusted, and a member that
-- arrived as neither is simply absent from every tally below. The two members read as
-- facts above are not arrays and so contribute nothing here, which is what lets one
-- gathered object carry both shapes.
reading AS (
  SELECT e.key AS node, x.item AS item
  FROM scope s,
       jsonb_each(s.nodes) e,
       jsonb_array_elements(
         CASE WHEN jsonb_typeof(e.value) = 'array'
              THEN e.value
              ELSE '[]'::jsonb
         END) AS x(item)
),

-- What the pass did, one count per question a reader of a digest asks. Every one of
-- them is a count over the reading above with a predicate, and the predicates are the
-- part worth reading: each is written against the shape its node actually answers.

-- findings_handed is the length of the list the caller sent and findings_selected is
-- how many of those became items. Select Scoring Subjects says the comparison belongs
-- here, and findings_dropped is the difference: a repeated id, an element that is not
-- an id, a finding no row holds, and a finding filed under another domain all land in
-- it, and nothing here says which. The causes are worth listing and the number is
-- worth reporting; attributing it would need the selection to answer what it did not
-- select.

-- documents_read, vectors_computed and vectors_reused count DOCUMENTS rather than
-- items. Two findings read out of one document share one vector, the node that
-- computes them memoising on the document id, so counting items would report the work
-- twice. vectors_reused is a document whose stored vector was already at the version
-- this domain's terms compose to, which is the skip that group exists for.

-- findings_scored and findings_unscored are complements over the same list and
-- together they are findings_selected. A score this pass could not take leaves both
-- columns on the finding alone, so unscored is work not done rather than work undone.

-- subjects_searchable and intentions_raised are the two lists the node above answers.
-- The first is how many findings carried a string somebody could search for and the
-- second how many new rows the pool gained, and the difference between them is the
-- findings an intention already cited.

-- signals_stated and signals_measured are the account of a score that no column
-- holds, and they are read as maxima because both are properties of the domain rather
-- than of a finding: the criteria list and the term set are the same for every item
-- in the pass. Stated at nought is a domain that has stated no criteria, and stated
-- above nought with measured at nought is a domain whose stated buckets are named by
-- none of its terms. They reach the errors entry below and no column.
tally AS (
  SELECT
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'handover') AS findings_handed,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'subjects') AS findings_selected,
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT (item ->> 'document_id')) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'vectors'
        AND (item ->> 'document_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$') AS documents_read,
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT (item ->> 'document_id')) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'vectors'
        AND (item ->> 'document_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
        AND item ->> 'feature_vector_source' = 'computed') AS vectors_computed,
    (SELECT count(DISTINCT (item ->> 'document_id')) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'vectors'
        AND (item ->> 'document_id') ~ '^[0-9]+$'
        AND item ->> 'feature_vector_source' = 'stored') AS vectors_reused,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'scores'
        AND COALESCE(item -> 'finding_scored' = 'true'::jsonb, false))
      AS findings_scored,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'scores'
        AND NOT COALESCE(item -> 'finding_scored' = 'true'::jsonb, false))
      AS findings_unscored,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'searchable') AS subjects_searchable,
    (SELECT count(*) FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'intentions') AS intentions_raised,
    (SELECT COALESCE(max((item ->> 'score_signals_stated')::integer), 0)
       FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'scores'
        AND (item ->> 'score_signals_stated') ~ '^[0-9]{1,9}$') AS signals_stated,
    (SELECT COALESCE(max((item ->> 'score_signals_measured')::integer), 0)
       FROM reading
      WHERE node = 'scores'
        AND (item ->> 'score_signals_measured') ~ '^[0-9]{1,9}$')
      AS signals_measured
),

-- What the pass could not do, one entry per failure, in the shape ar-dispatch's Close
-- Run Failed already writes: the node that met it and the values that say what it
-- was. The ordinal is what keeps two passes failing the same way reporting in the
-- same order.

-- Two entries, and a pass can carry both at once. A hand over naming findings this
-- canvas could not select is one, and findings it selected and could not measure is
-- the other.
failure AS (
  SELECT
    1 AS ordinal,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'node', 'Select Scoring Subjects',
      'findings_handed', t.findings_handed,
      'findings_selected', t.findings_selected) AS entry
  FROM tally t
  WHERE t.findings_handed > t.findings_selected

  UNION ALL

  SELECT
    2 AS ordinal,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'node', 'Aggregate Finding Scores',
      'findings_unscored', t.findings_unscored,
      'signals_stated', t.signals_stated,
      'signals_measured', t.signals_measured) AS entry
  FROM tally t
  WHERE t.findings_unscored > 0
),

-- The three things the insert writes, worked out before it runs so that the statement
-- below is a write and not a decision.
outcome AS (
  SELECT
    CASE
      WHEN t.findings_selected > 0 AND t.findings_scored = 0
        THEN 'failed'
      WHEN t.findings_unscored > 0 OR t.findings_handed > t.findings_selected
        THEN 'partial'
      ELSE 'ok'
    END AS status,
    jsonb_build_object(
      'findings_handed', t.findings_handed,
      'findings_selected', t.findings_selected,
      'findings_dropped', t.findings_handed - t.findings_selected,
      'documents_read', t.documents_read,
      'vectors_computed', t.vectors_computed,
      'vectors_reused', t.vectors_reused,
      'findings_scored', t.findings_scored,
      'findings_unscored', t.findings_unscored,
      'subjects_searchable', t.subjects_searchable,
      'intentions_raised', t.intentions_raised) AS counts,
    COALESCE(
      (SELECT jsonb_agg(f.entry ORDER BY f.ordinal, f.entry) FROM failure f),
      '[]'::jsonb) AS entries
  FROM tally t
),

-- The write. Six columns and no others: id and started_at are the table's own, and
-- there is nothing else on a runs row.

-- status and finished_at are set together because nothing in the schema holds them
-- together. A row saying failed with no finish, or carrying a finish while still
-- saying running, is storable, and runs.status records that only the writer pairs
-- them. Here they are written by one statement and the row is never reopened.
opened AS (
  INSERT INTO runs (domain_id, scheduled_by, status, finished_at, counts, errors)
  SELECT s.domain_id, 'operator', o.status, now(), o.counts, o.entries
  FROM scope s, outcome o
  RETURNING id
)

SELECT
-- The item this node answers, and the last one this workflow emits. Both callers
-- receive it, each through an Execute Workflow node that waits for this workflow, and
-- each reads it for an error member that is only there when the invocation did not
-- complete. Everything else on it is the execution's own record.

-- There is no did-it-land member here, where every other write on this canvas carries
-- one. The insert is unconditional and its RETURNING is read straight out, so a run
-- id IS the answer: the row exists or the statement raised, and there is no third
-- outcome for a member to report.

-- counts and status travel because they are what this node decided, and reading them
-- back off the answer is cheaper than reading the row again. The feature version and
-- whether it matches the domain's pin travel for the reason the header gives, this
-- being the execution record they were carried this far to reach.
  (SELECT o.id FROM opened o) AS run_id,
  s.domain_id,
  o.status,
  o.counts,
  jsonb_array_length(o.entries) AS errors_recorded,
  s.feature_version,
  s.feature_version_matches_domain
FROM scope s, outcome o

options.queryReplacement: ={{ JSON.stringify({ context: { domain_id: $('Load Domain Context').first().json.domain_id }, generation: { feature_version: $('Write Finding Scores').first().json.feature_version, matches_domain: $('Write Finding Scores').first().json.feature_version_matches_domain }, handover: $('Execute Workflow Trigger').first().json.finding_ids ?? [], subjects: $('Select Scoring Subjects').all().map((item) => item.json.finding_id), vectors: $('Compute Feature Vectors').all().map((item) => ({ document_id: item.json.document_id, feature_vector_source: item.json.feature_vector_source })), scores: $('Write Finding Scores').all().map((item) => ({ finding_scored: item.json.finding_scored, score_signals_stated: item.json.score_signals_stated, score_signals_measured: item.json.score_signals_measured })), searchable: $('Raise Research Intentions').first().json.searchable_finding_ids, intentions: $('Raise Research Intentions').first().json.intention_ids }) }}

parameters.content:
## Two Callers, No Clock

This workflow is invoked, and by two workflows rather than by the dispatcher. `ar-ingest` reaches it at the end of a pull pass and `ar-capture` at the end of a push one, each through an Execute Workflow node that waits for it. `ar-dispatch` does not invoke it at all, and nothing schedules a scoring pass: a pass exists where findings were just written, which is a thing that has happened rather than a time that has come.

It holds no clock and may not acquire one: `ar-dispatch` carries the only Schedule Trigger in the system, and `tests/invariants/workflows.test.ts` counts them across every built workflow and names the one file allowed to hold one. The Execute Workflow Trigger here registers nothing when a workflow is activated, so `scripts/activate-workflows.sh` reports this file manual-only and leaves it inactive. That is the outcome rather than a gap: what starts this workflow is a caller, and a caller needs no registration.

### What arrives

One item, and three members of it are the hand-over. `domain_id` says whose criteria to score against, `finding_ids` says exactly which rows, and one provenance member says which pass wrote them: `ingest_run_id` from one caller, `capture_document_id` from the other.

Neither of those is spelled `run_id`, and both callers say why on the nodes that write them. A member with that name is what a first node written to this shape resolves its domain out of, and the run this workflow will account for is its own rather than the caller's. So provenance travels under a name that cannot be mistaken for one, and nothing in the schema keeps the two apart.

`Load Domain Context` reads the first of the three and no more. The subject list stays where it arrived, reachable at `$('Execute Workflow Trigger').first().json`, and reading it belongs to the group that selects the findings rather than to the node that fetches the taxonomy.

### Started by hand

A run started from this canvas rather than by a caller carries no `domain_id`, and nothing pretends otherwise. `Load Domain Context` answers a null `domain_id`, a null domain row and four empty lists, which is a shape every node below can read. `Select Scoring Subjects` reads it by selecting nothing: a null domain matches no finding, so a pass with no domain scores nothing rather than scoring a corpus against a position nobody stated.

That is one of three ways this canvas ends early, and the other two are ordinary rather than a mistake: a hand over naming no finding reaches the same zero, and so does one naming only findings filed under another domain. `ar-capture` invokes this workflow for every capture including the ones that wrote no finding, and says on the node that does so that what a scoring pass makes of an empty list is this workflow's answer rather than its own. The answer is that a node handed no item does not run, so the pass stops above the group built to account for it. Nothing here suppresses that and nothing here can fix it: every node on this canvas sits on one main chain, and a branch off the context node is the canvas topology's repair rather than any one node's.

nodes.name: A Null Score Is Not A Zero

parameters.content:
## A Null Score Is Not A Zero

`findings.score` is nullable with no default, and this group is the only thing holding the rule that column states: a number computed from data is absent rather than zero when nothing measured it. `Aggregate Finding Scores` decides which of the two a finding gets, and `Write Finding Scores` writes the pair or writes neither column.

### What counts as measured

A domain states its position as `criteria` rows, each filed under one of its categories, and `domains.settings.scoringWeights` says what each bucket is worth. The reading for a bucket is the count `features.ts` put in that bucket's column of the vector, taken over the document behind the finding.

A bucket whose column the vector carries is measured, and a count of nothing there is a measured `0` that is stored like any other number. The domain's terms were run over the document and matched none of them, which is a reading and not an absence.

### What counts as absent

A bucket the domain asks about and gives the pipeline no term to match it with has no column in the vector at all, because `features.ts` gives a category a column when a term names it and not otherwise. Nothing read it, so nothing is reported about it, and `toFinite` in `aggregate-score.ts` is what keeps that apart from a zero on the way into the sum.

Three shapes reach a finding with no measurable signal, and all three are facts about the domain's configuration rather than about the finding: a domain that has stated no criteria, a domain whose stated buckets are named by none of its terms, and a domain that has stated no share for any of them. Each answers `null`, and the statement below then writes neither column.

### What a zero would cost

An unscored finding stored as `0` takes its place at the bottom of every ranking as though it had been read and found worthless, and nothing downstream can tell it from a finding genuinely scored to nothing. A `score >= 0.7` threshold evaluates to UNKNOWN against a NULL and so neither takes an unscored finding nor reports it, which is right, because nothing has measured it. The same finding stored as `0` is taken and reported, as a measurement nobody made.

### What is left alone

A finding this pass could not measure keeps whatever it already had. The write is guarded on this pass's answer rather than on the row, so a finding scored under an earlier scheme keeps that score and the version that dates it. Blanking it would discard a reading somebody took in favour of one nobody did.
